title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N = 300 matched intents) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations from an LLM intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen protocol that used a shared_initial_candidate generation contract and two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, the run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). Paired risk-difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Because validators never reported violations, no repair call was invoked and the experiment cannot evaluate repair efficacy. Observing 0/300 violations gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. We present concise methodological definitions (including the operational forbidden-reachability predicate and validator assumptions), a compact numerical results summary, and artifact pointers for verification to guide follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises security concerns: generated artifacts can inadvertently expand attack surface or violate access-control intentions. Prior system and survey work therefore recommends constrained generation, execution oracles, and generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. Yet preregistered, paired evaluations that quantify whether embedding a verifier reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations under adversarial intents are scarce. We therefore posed the confirmatory question that drove a preregistered experiment: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our evidence-grounded contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired N = 300 confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1); (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution under a shared_initial_candidate contract and two deterministic validators; (3) a compact, artifact-verified report of a degenerate confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300) with exact inferential quantities and a Clopper–Pearson bound on undetected violation rate; and (4) design recommendations and reproducibility pointers to support follow-up stress tests that exercise the repair path. Notation: ‘baseline’ is the shared initial LLM candidate replayed directly; ‘guarded’ is the same candidate validated and allowed up to one repair call if a validator detects forbidden reachability.
sections.related_work: Research on verifier-guided repair and execution-guided architectures shows substantial correctness gains in code and Infrastructure-as-Code tasks when verifier feedback guides repairs (e.g., TerraFormer and related verifier-feedback systems) [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Surveys of LLMs for NetOps document recurring failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce operational risk [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Emulation and testbed work demonstrates the feasibility of execution-based validation but cautions about external-validity gaps when moving to production devices and live traffic [https://openalex.org/W4406170828]. Our study differs by preregistering a paired confirmatory design, executing deterministically, and archiving per-episode validator traces to make the limits of the confirmatory inference explicit.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: The study (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intent pairs (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). Prespecified 95% bootstrap percentile CIs were planned; final analysis used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) to reduce Monte Carlo variability. Sampling included deterministic deduplication rules (exact duplicates removed; fuzzy duplicates with normalized edit distance < 0.15 excluded) as recorded in the archived task manifest.

Forbidden-reachability predicate and validator summaries (concise, operational): The forbidden-reachability predicate was operationalized for this experiment as any emulator-observed change in final forwarding/ACL state that newly permits traffic from an external/untrusted endpoint to reach interfaces explicitly listed as protected in the task payloads (protected_interfaces; e.g., "mgmt1" in the archived tasks). Concretely, a violation occurs when the validator-detected final state shows reachability that was not present in the initial state and that grants access to a protected interface contrary to the task constraints. Two deterministic validators implemented this check: (1) a containerized execution validator (Batfish-style) that materializes the generated configuration into an FRRouting-style emulator, computes induced forwarding/ACL state, and issues reachability queries against that concrete state; and (2) a lightweight static graph-based reachability analyzer implemented in Python that analyzes command-level changes and infers allowed flows via a graph abstraction. The experiment combined validator outputs with a logical OR decision rule: a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports forbidden reachability. Validator identifiers and per-episode traces are archived under execution/scoring/*.json (validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version = '5.0'). Known limitations: the execution validator depends on the emulator's fidelity to data-plane behavior; the static analyzer can underdetect complex dynamic routing/ACL interactions. These detection assumptions and limitations are summarized here and the per-episode validator_trace files provide full operational detail for auditors.

Adapter contract and generation semantics: To conserve model calls under the execution contract we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent pair a single initial LLM candidate was generated and replayed to both arms (one hosted-model generation per pair). The preregistration allowed up to one repair LLM call on guarded pairs if a validator detected a forbidden reachability; repair calls were never invoked in the run because validators never reported violations. Provider-call accounting (execution/execution_manifest.json) records model_calls_used = 300 under this contract. Analysis: primary McNemar paired test plus 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples). We also computed a descriptive one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound for the baseline violation probability given 0 observed violations.
sections.results:
Execution summary (compact): planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300 (shared_initial_candidate). Primary outcome (Table 1): contingency n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p-value = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) for the paired difference = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on the baseline violation rate. Because no validator detected forbidden reachability for any initial candidate, no repair prompt was issued and repair_applied = false across all archived per-episode validator traces; verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in the archived artifacts. Median guarded-model-call overhead under the shared contract is 0 (repair path unused).

Compact verification pointers: the complete reproducibility bundle is archived; representative artifacts for immediate verification include execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256: 36ea4a5dfa90384f2a388cba4f39bf193bb3c150ea22ca60957facb20ca960f1), and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (sha256: 62bd1fe90a9ad7b2798d5241c3c52404750cbab678e6b92692d2cc2bae2356bf). The execution manifest and per-episode scoring traces (execution/scoring/*.json) contain the provider-call audit, validator_trace entries (including repair_applied flags), and normalized final states used for scoring.
sections.discussion:
What is supported: Under the preregistered adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), deterministic emulator, and the two validators combined by logical OR, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for every sampled intent; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The archived per-episode validator_trace entries, provider-call audit, and analysis contingency are mutually consistent and support this narrow, artifact-grounded conclusion.

What is not supported: Because the repair path was never exercised, the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction; the degenerate observed contingency (no discordant pairs) violates that assumption and makes McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy.

Design lessons and operational implications (artifact-grounded): (1) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate reduces provider cost (model_calls_used = 300 vs up to 600 for independent draws) but also reduces between-arm variability required to observe repair-rescuable discordant cases. For experiments that aim to exercise repair efficacy, independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or larger sample sizes/repair budgets are recommended. (2) Adversary potency matters: programmatic single-variant adversaries used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability; stronger, targeted adversaries are needed to stress repair. (3) Verifier diversity and fidelity matter: combining multiple oracle families and production-grade oracles will better exercise different failure modes. All these trade-offs are directly observable in the archived execution manifest and task manifest that record generation semantics, model-call budgets, and task payloads.
sections.conclusion: This preregistered paired evaluation shows that, under the exact frozen contract used here (shared initial candidate, gpt-5-mini, two deterministic validators), baseline generation already satisfied the operational forbidden-reachability predicate for the sampled intents and therefore inserting the verifier did not alter observed compliance (n11 = 300). Because no repair calls occurred, the experiment cannot adjudicate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue violating outputs. We release the preregistration, deterministic execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducible reanalysis and to inform follow-up stress tests (independent-condition generation, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and higher repair budgets) that can exercise the repair path and test the original confirmatory hypothesis.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; preregistered power assumptions are not met.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and transformation logs are available in the execution bundle for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetic and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
